content: Oral candidiasis, also known as thrush, is a fungal infection of the mouth and throat caused by an overgrowth of Candida species. Candida yeasts are typically present in small amounts on the skin and mucous membranes without causing harm. However, when the environment in the mouth or throat becomes imbalanced, these yeasts can proliferate, leading to symptoms. In some cases, Candida overgrowth can extend to the esophagus, resulting in esophageal candidiasis. The first description of a yeast-like fungus associated with oral thrush was made in 1839 by B. Lagenbeck in Germany, who identified its role in causing the infection. Candida species, including Candida albicans, are normal inhabitants of the mouth, throat, and gastrointestinal tract. Under typical conditions, they coexist with the body without causing disease. However, factors such as immunosuppression or the use of certain medications can disrupt this balance, allowing Candida to multiply and cause infection. Oral candidiasis is primarily caused by Candida albicans, though less commonly, other species such as Candida glabrata, Candida tropicalis, Candida parapsilosis, or Candida krusei may be involved. These fungi infect the mucous membranes of the mouth. It is important to differentiate oropharyngeal candidiasis from other forms of oral candidiasis and from other diseases that can cause similar symptoms, such as stomatitis or glossitis. Oral candidiasis is not common in the general population but is frequently diagnosed in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS, cancer, or other conditions that weaken the immune system. Certain risk factors increase the likelihood of developing oral thrush. For example, individuals with diabetes and poorly controlled blood sugar levels are at higher risk because the excess sugar in saliva provides a substrate for Candida growth. Prolonged or high-dose antibiotic use can also predispose individuals to thrush by disrupting the balance of healthy bacteria that normally inhibit Candida overgrowth. Additionally, poorly fitting dentures can increase the risk of oral thrush. With appropriate antifungal therapy, oral candidiasis typically resolves without long-term complications. However, in immunocompromised patients with disseminated Candida infections, the mortality rate can approach 50%. In infants, oral thrush may cause discomfort and interfere with feeding, but it is rarely serious. If symptoms persist for more than two weeks, a pediatrician should be consulted. In adults, oral thrush is generally curable, but the prognosis depends on the underlying immune status and the cause of immune suppression. In severely immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV or undergoing chemotherapy, Candida can spread systemically, causing infections in the esophagus (esophagitis), brain (meningitis), heart (endocarditis), joints (arthritis), or eyes (endophthalmitis). Adults with oral candidiasis may experience discomfort or a burning sensation in the mouth. Esophageal candidiasis can cause pain and difficulty swallowing (dysphagia). The most common symptom of oral thrush is the presence of white patches or plaques on the tongue and other oral mucous membranes. On physical examination, oral Candida infections typically appear as thick white or cream-colored deposits. The mucosa underlying these deposits may be inflamed, appearing red and possibly slightly raised. Oral lesions are usually painless and present as white patches in the mouth. Diagnosis is based on clinical symptoms and confirmed by microscopic examination of scrapings from affected areas. A culture may also be performed, but since Candida is a normal inhabitant of the mouth, a positive culture alone is not diagnostic. Treatment of oral candidiasis involves the use of topical antifungal agents such as nystatin, miconazole, or amphotericin B. In immunocompromised patients, systemic antifungal therapy with oral or intravenous medications may be required. Primary prevention strategies include maintaining good oral hygiene, which can help reduce the risk of oral thrush in individuals with weakened immune systems. Studies have shown that chlorhexidine (CHX) mouthwash may help prevent oral candidiasis in patients undergoing cancer treatment. For individuals using inhaled corticosteroids, rinsing the mouth with water or mouthwash after using an inhaler can reduce the risk of developing thrush. Secondary prevention is generally not necessary, as Candida infections are usually self-limiting unless there is concurrent immunosuppression.
